# Ask What the Fitted Model Would Generate

A posterior distribution can be computed accurately even when the model fails
to represent important features of the data. Posterior predictive checking asks
whether replicated data generated from the fitted model resemble the observed
data in ways that matter for the scientific analysis.

For observed data $y$, parameters $\theta$, and a replicate $y^{\mathrm{rep}}$
generated under the same observation process, the posterior predictive
distribution is

$$
\boxed{
p(y^{\mathrm{rep}}\mid y)
=\int p(y^{\mathrm{rep}}\mid\theta)
p(\theta\mid y)\,d\theta.
}
$$

Simulation follows the factorization:

$$
\theta^{(s)}\sim p(\theta\mid y),
\qquad
y^{\mathrm{rep},(s)}\sim p(y^{\mathrm{rep}}\mid\theta^{(s)}).
$$

The replicate must preserve the design being checked: sample sizes, covariates,
exposures, missingness assumptions, clustering, and measurement process. A
check is a comparison, not a binary proof that a model is true or false.

# Prediction Target Determines the Replicate

“New data” can mean different things in a hierarchical study:

| Predictive target | What is held fixed? | What is regenerated? | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| New measurement in an observed unit | unit effect and design | observation noise | another assay of the same donor sample |
| New observation for an observed group | group parameter | outcome conditional on that group | another time point for an enrolled donor |
| New group from the population | population parameters | group effect and outcomes | a new donor from the target population |
| Replication of the full study | design mechanism or design variables | groups, latent effects, and outcomes | a new multi-donor experiment |

These distributions answer different questions. A conditional check may fit
within-group noise while missing excessive between-group heterogeneity. A
new-group check may expose that failure. State the replication thought experiment
before interpreting the comparison.

# Choose Discrepancies That Can Reveal Consequential Failures

A test quantity $T(y)$ reduces the data to a feature worth checking. Useful
choices follow from the estimand, likelihood, scientific mechanism, and known
failure modes rather than from whatever plot is easiest to produce.

Examples include:

- location, spread, skewness, tails, and extreme values;
- the number of zeros, detection frequency, and saturation;
- a mean--variance or abundance--dispersion relationship;
- residual association with fitted values, time, batch, or sequencing depth;
- within- and between-unit variability;
- autocorrelation, spatial clustering, or run lengths;
- group contrasts, rank patterns, or the statistic driving a decision; and
- the fraction of observations outside a scientifically meaningful range.

No single discrepancy is omnibus. A model may reproduce the mean while missing
tails, or match marginal counts while missing donor-level dependence. Inspect
several prespecified, interpretable features, including the quantity most closely
connected to the substantive conclusion.

# Graphical Checks

Graphical posterior predictive checks retain more structure than one-number
summaries. Common comparisons are:

- observed histograms, empirical distribution functions, or density estimates
  overlaid on a manageable set of predictive draws;
- observed statistics against predictive intervals for each group;
- binned residual or calibration plots against important predictors;
- predictive distributions of maxima, zero counts, slopes, or variance ratios;
  and
- small multiples stratified by treatment, batch, site, sex, ancestry, or time.

Plotting hundreds of opaque replicated curves can conceal rather than reveal
misfit. Show predictive intervals or a limited set of draws, mark the observed
quantity clearly, and preserve units. Group-specific plots are important because
aggregation can make poor subgroup fit disappear.

# Numerical Discrepancies and Posterior Predictive P-values

A posterior predictive tail-area probability can be written

$$
p_B
=P\!\left[T(y^{\mathrm{rep}})\ge T(y)\mid y\right]
\approx
\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S
I\!\left\{T(y^{\mathrm{rep},(s)})\ge T(y)\right\}.
$$

Values near 0 or 1 can flag systematic discrepancy in the chosen direction.
This quantity is not an ordinary frequentist $p$-value. The observed data are
used both to form the posterior and to evaluate the discrepancy, so posterior
predictive $p$-values are generally not uniform under the model and often
concentrate toward $0.5$. A threshold such as 0.05 therefore should not be used
as a universal accept/reject rule.

When a discrepancy depends on the parameter, use
$T(y,\theta^{(s)})$ and compare it with
$T(y^{\mathrm{rep},(s)},\theta^{(s)})$ within each draw. Report the discrepancy,
direction, simulation precision, and practical importance of the mismatch.

# A Worked Beta--Binomial Check

Suppose donor $j$ has $n_j$ reads informative for an allele and $y_j$ alternate
reads. A simple binomial model is

$$
y_j\mid p\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,p),
\qquad
p\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b).
$$

After drawing $p^{(s)}$ from the posterior, simulate

$$
y_j^{\mathrm{rep},(s)}\sim
\operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,p^{(s)}).
$$

A discrepancy sensitive to extra donor heterogeneity is the sample variance of
the observed allele fractions:

$$
T(y)=\operatorname{Var}_j\left(\frac{y_j}{n_j}\right).
$$

If $T(y)$ is repeatedly larger than its posterior predictive replicates, a
shared $p$ plus binomial sampling does not generate enough between-donor
variation. A beta--binomial or hierarchical model may be appropriate, but the
revision should follow the scientific source of heterogeneity. Unmodeled ancestry,
batch, copy-number state, or contamination should not be hidden automatically
inside an overdispersion parameter.

The donor remains the biological unit. Reads measure each donor's fraction and
do not supply independent evidence about variation among donors.

# Prior and Posterior Predictive Checks Have Different Jobs

The prior predictive distribution is

$$
p(y)=\int p(y\mid\theta)p(\theta)\,d\theta.
$$

It checks whether the model and prior generate scientifically plausible data
before the observed outcomes influence inference. It can reveal impossible
scales, excessive concentration, or interactions among weakly specified priors.

The posterior predictive distribution conditions on $y$ and asks whether the
fitted model can reproduce relevant features. Passing a posterior check does not
validate the prior: a strong likelihood can overwhelm implausible prior regions.
Conversely, prior predictive breadth is not model flexibility after fitting.
Both checks belong in a Bayesian workflow.

# Predictive Residuals and Calibration

Raw residuals $y_i-E(y_i\mid y)$ may be difficult to compare when variance and
support change with predictors. Alternatives include standardized residuals,
randomized quantile residuals for discrete outcomes, and predictive probability
integral transform values. Their reference behavior depends on whether the
prediction reuses the observation being assessed.

In-sample posterior prediction is optimistic for detecting overfitting because
each observation helps fit its own predictive distribution. Leave-one-out or
held-out predictive checks instead compare $y_i$ with

$$
p(y_i\mid y_{-i})
=\int p(y_i\mid\theta)p(\theta\mid y_{-i})\,d\theta.
$$

These checks are valuable for predictive calibration and influential
observations. They answer a different question from ordinary posterior checks,
which are often better at diagnosing whether a particular generative assumption
can reproduce a chosen data feature. Cross-validation compares out-of-sample
prediction; it does not replace scientific model criticism.

# Computation Must Be Valid Before Model Checking

Posterior predictive simulation inherits errors from posterior computation.
Before interpreting a check:

- resolve divergent transitions and other sampler warnings;
- inspect rank-normalized split $\widehat R$ and bulk/tail effective sample sizes;
- ensure enough effective draws for the tail area or predictive quantile;
- quantify Monte Carlo error when it could change the conclusion; and
- verify that the replication code implements the same likelihood, offsets,
  censoring, and missing-data rules as the fitted model.

Duplicating posterior draws does not add information. For rare predictive events,
simulate additional independent outcomes conditional on well-explored posterior
draws or improve posterior sampling, and report the remaining numerical
uncertainty.

# From Discrepancy to Model Revision

A useful check suggests where the generative story fails. Revisions may include:

| Observed discrepancy | Possible mechanism | Targeted revision or sensitivity analysis |
|---|---|---|
| more zeros than predicted | structural absence, censoring, or low exposure | model detection/absence separately; check exposure and threshold assumptions |
| heavier tails | outliers, latent mixtures, or underestimated measurement error | robust likelihood, mixture, or explicit error model |
| variance rises too quickly with the mean | overdispersion or omitted heterogeneity | dispersion model, group effects, or relevant covariates |
| residual batch pattern | unmodeled technical process or confounding | add batch structure; examine overlap and design limitations |
| serial or spatial residual dependence | missing correlation or dynamic process | correlation, state-space, or spatial model |
| poor new-group prediction | wrong population distribution or exchangeability claim | covariates, robust hierarchy, stratification, or narrower target population |

Model revision should be scientifically interpretable. Repeatedly adding
parameters until familiar plots look acceptable can overfit the observed data.
Recheck revised models, evaluate sensitivity, and use held-out prediction when
prediction is the goal. Preserve a record of the iterative workflow.

# What Posterior Predictive Checks Cannot Establish

- **They do not prove a model is true.** Many incompatible models reproduce the
  same selected summaries.
- **They do not identify causality.** Confounding, selection, and measurement
  assumptions can remain invisible in the observed distribution.
- **They do not validate priors by themselves.** Posterior conditioning may hide
  implausible prior implications.
- **They do not choose the estimand.** A well-fitting read-level model may still
  answer the wrong donor-level question.
- **They do not repair pseudoreplication.** An observation model cannot create
  independent biological units.
- **They do not rank models on one universal scale.** Predictive accuracy,
  calibration, interpretability, and scientific adequacy are distinct criteria.

# Bioinformatics Workflow

For a multi-donor single-cell or bulk RNA-seq analysis:

1. Identify donors or independently assigned samples as experimental units;
   classify cells, reads, and repeated assays as lower-level or technical units.
2. Define the biological estimand, such as a donor-population log fold change,
   and the conditions to which it generalizes.
3. Check priors by simulating library sizes, zero frequencies, dispersions, and
   plausible fold changes before fitting.
4. Validate [MCMC computation](bayesian-computation-mcmc.qmd).
5. Simulate replicated counts with the observed design matrix and offsets.
6. Compare abundance--variance trends, zero counts, tails, treatment contrasts,
   donor heterogeneity, and batch-resolved summaries.
7. Refit defensible alternatives and report whether the statistical conclusion
   and biological interpretation change.

A statistical statement might be that the fitted negative-binomial hierarchy
underpredicts donor-to-donor variability. The biological interpretation requires
investigating whether that variation reflects genuine heterogeneity, batch,
composition, or measurement. These are not interchangeable explanations.

# Connections and Take-home Messages

- [Bayesian priors, likelihoods, and posteriors](../statistical-inference/bayesian-priors-likelihoods-and-posteriors.qmd)
  provides the update underlying posterior prediction.
- [Bayesian computation: MCMC](bayesian-computation-mcmc.qmd) supplies posterior
  draws and computational diagnostics.
- [Hierarchical Bayesian models](hierarchical-bayesian-models.qmd) distinguishes
  within-unit, observed-group, and new-group predictions.
- [Partial pooling and exchangeability](partial-pooling-and-exchangeability.qmd)
  clarifies what population a replicated group represents.
- [Cross-validation](../regression-models/cross-validation.qmd) evaluates
  out-of-sample predictive performance with the appropriate resampling unit.
- [Sensitivity analysis and robustness](../statistical-inference/sensitivity-analysis-and-robustness.qmd)
  asks whether conclusions survive plausible model changes.

Posterior predictive checking compares observed features with data generated by
the fitted model. Its value comes from a clearly defined replication target,
discrepancies connected to scientific consequences, valid computation, and
transparent model revision. A check can reveal a failure the analyst thought to
look for; it cannot certify every unexamined assumption.
